idiom_name: impl From<&UserDto> for User (TryFrom where a field can be invalid)
implementation_notes: Rust dissolves the mapper object into the stdlib conversion protocol: implement `From<&UserDto> for User` - or `TryFrom<&UserDto> for User` when a field can be invalid - and `Into`/`into()` follows from the blanket impl, so the boundary writes `let user: User = dto.into()`. The rules still live in one place, the impl block, and the target's struct literal makes an added field a compile error, which is exactly the drift protection hand-written mappers elsewhere lack. Use `TryFrom` for anything crossing a trust boundary (unknown enum variants, ranges, absent required fields) and `From` only for total conversions; keep the impls free of I/O so they stay testable and usable from `collect()`.
pitfalls: `From` cannot fail: mapping a fallible field (unknown enum variant, out-of-range number) through `From` invents a default and loses the error - use `TryFrom`.
Orphan rules force the impl to live where one of the two types is defined; put DTO types in the boundary crate (or wrap foreign types in a local newtype) instead of fighting the compiler.
Cloning every string field is easy to write and hard to notice; take `&Dto` and clone deliberately, or accept owned DTOs by value when the caller has finished with them.

variants.name: Attribute-driven mapping with serde
variants.idiom_name: serde derive with #[serde(rename / default / try_from)] attributes
variants.implementation_notes: When the other representation is serde's data model (JSON, YAML, MessagePack), the derive macro becomes the mapper: `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` plus `#[serde(rename = "full_name")]`, `default`, `skip_serializing_if` and `try_from = "UserDto"` declares the mapping next to the DTO, and the boundary only calls `serde_json::from_str` / `to_string`. The rules are still yours, but they become attributes rather than code, and `try_from` routes the DTO through a `TryFrom` impl when validation is required. Keep serde types in the boundary crate rather than the domain - the derive adds a dependency and a wire schema to every type that carries it - and hand-write the conversion when the mapping computes rather than renames.
pitfalls: Attributes are invisible at the call site: a renamed or defaulted field changes the wire contract without touching any function body, so contract tests are the only guard.
`deny_unknown_fields` is a container-level decision and conflicts with flattening; an evolving producer makes it fail closed on additions.
The derive pulls serde into every type that carries it, so annotating domain types leaks a serialization dependency into the core.
